title: Catherine's Dialogue
hookLine: Catherine dictates her book to secretaries while deep in prayer
carry: prayer is a conversation, not a speech
tomorrow: how do you cross a river when the old road has washed out?

lines: WHY DOES IT SAY A SOUL?
cards: Half of what gets written now is spoken: voice notes, talk-to-text, a phone held up while someone paces the kitchen. Catherine of Siena has a book made a little like that.
The people around her said she spoke it aloud, deep in prayer, while secretaries took it down. Which makes the first page strange. It never says I.
It says a soul. Why would a woman dictating her own book talk about herself as someone else?

teach.b: Clue one, the opening. The Dialogue begins with a soul lifted up by a great desire for the honor of God and the good of others, and that soul brings her requests to God. No name, no I.

teach.h: THE SOUL ASKS; THE FATHER ANSWERS.
teach.b: It's called the Dialogue because that's what it is: the soul asks, and God the Father answers, often at length, calling her his dearest daughter. Most of the pages are in his voice, not hers. Clue three, the person.
By stepping out of the first person, Catherine moves herself out of the center. One way to read it: the asking soul could be any soul, and the reader is invited into that seat. Clue four, the method.
If the people around her are right that she spoke it from prayer, then the book wasn't drafted and then prayed over.
The praying and the speaking were the same act, and others caught the words as they came.
So the puzzle solves itself. A book that comes out of a conversation with God is written in the voice of a conversation, and the one talking isn't the hero of it.
Catholics honor Catherine as a saint and a Doctor of the Church, and the Dialogue is the book she's best known for.

how: Catholics read Catherine of Siena's Dialogue as a classic of prayer; some read it slowly, a section at a time, as a conversation they're invited into.

games.q: you're Catherine. your companions are ready to write down what comes to you in prayer. how should the book sound?
o: like a diary: what i did, what i felt, how holy it was.
like a conversation: a soul asks, and God the Father answers.
like a rulebook: ten steps that guarantee holiness.
games.why: the Dialogue says a soul, not I, and most of its pages are in the Father's voice. for Catholics, prayer is a two-way relationship with God, not a speech.

practice: Prayer, in Catherine's book, has two voices, so try both halves. Say one line out loud, quietly, almost a whisper: a line of a psalm, the Our Father, or a plain sentence of what's true for you right now. Then stop talking.

Stay in the quiet it leaves, as the soul in the Dialogue waits for the answer, and notice whatever comes, even if it's only stillness. If you don't pray, say the line to the quiet itself, and listen the same way.

wordCard.voice: Dictated in prayer. Catherine's book, spoken aloud from prayer, as her companions told it, and taken down by others.
